resources.description: Kubernetes node pool, 24 x D8s v5
resources.finding: Every node in this pool bills at pay-as-you-go rates. The pool has not dropped below 20 nodes in six months, so 20 of the 24 nodes are effectively permanent capacity being rented by the hour.

current_config.label: terraform/aks.tf (current)
current_config.code:
resource "azurerm_kubernetes_cluster_node_pool" "prod3" {
  name                  = "nodepool3"
  vm_size               = "Standard_D8s_v5"
  node_count            = 24
  enable_auto_scaling   = true
  min_count             = 20
  max_count             = 32
  priority              = "Regular"   # pay-as-you-go, billed hourly
}

change.label: Buy a 1-year savings plan for the stable floor

maths: 20 nodes never released in 6 months = the committed floor
20 / 24 nodes x $19,840 = $16,533 of the bill is stable capacity
Azure 1-year compute savings plan on D-series = about 34% off pay-as-you-go
$16,533 x 0.34 = $5,621, rounded down to $5,550 to allow for rate drift
resources.risk: A savings plan is a one-year financial commitment. If the pool is retired early the commitment still bills. Covering only the 20-node floor keeps the burst capacity flexible.
resources.effort: One purchase, no deployment, no downtime.

resources.finding: Training jobs run on on-demand A100s, and the pool floor is 2 nodes so it never scales to zero. Job logs show 94% of runs are checkpointed every 15 minutes, which means they survive preemption and do not need on-demand capacity.

current_config.label: terraform/gke-ml.tf (current)

change.label: Spot capacity for checkpointed jobs, and a true zero floor

maths: Pool ran 19 of 31 days; 12 idle days still billed the 2-node floor
Floor waste: 2/8 nodes x 12/31 days x $17,220 = $1,666
Active spend on the 19 running days = $15,554
94% of runs are checkpointed and can move to spot
$15,554 x 0.94 x 0.45 average spot discount = $6,579
$1,666 + $6,579 = $8,245, rounded to $8,270 against current spot rates
resources.risk: Spot nodes can be reclaimed with 30 seconds notice. Only jobs that checkpoint should tolerate the taint. The 6% of runs that do not checkpoint stay on an on-demand pool.
resources.effort: One Terraform apply plus a toleration added to the training job template. Roughly half a day.

resources.finding: The scale set is correctly autoscaling and is not oversized. The only saving here is rate, not shape: the 6-instance floor has never been breached downward in a year.

current_config.label: terraform/api-vmss.tf (current)

change.label: Reserve the floor only
change.code:
# Extend the existing savings plan to cover the 6-instance floor.
# No change to the scale set or the autoscale rules.

#   6 x Standard_D4s_v5, 1-year term, region eastus
#   Leaves instances 7-20 on pay-as-you-go so bursts stay elastic.

maths: 6 of an average 11 running instances are permanent = 55% of the bill
$13,405 x 0.55 = $7,373 of stable capacity
1-year savings plan on D4s v5 = about 26% off
resources.risk: Same one-year commitment risk as the AKS pool. Low, because the API tier is not scheduled for replacement.

resources.finding: The tier is correct - billing genuinely needs the availability guarantees of Business Critical. But the instance runs at pay-as-you-go rates and has been unchanged for two years, and Azure Hybrid Benefit is not applied despite the licences being owned.

current_config.label: terraform/sql-mi.tf (current)
current_config.code:
resource "azurerm_mssql_managed_instance" "billing" {
  name             = "sql-mi-billing-prod"
  sku_name         = "BC_Gen5"
  vcores           = 16
  storage_size_in_gb = 2048
  license_type     = "LicenseIncluded"   # paying for SQL licences twice
}

change.label: Apply owned licences, then reserve the capacity
change.code:
resource "azurerm_mssql_managed_instance" "billing" {
  name             = "sql-mi-billing-prod"
  sku_name         = "BC_Gen5"
  vcores           = 16
  storage_size_in_gb = 2048
  license_type     = "BasePrice"   # Azure Hybrid Benefit - use owned licences
}

# Then a 1-year reserved capacity purchase for 16 vCores, BC_Gen5, eastus.

maths: Azure Hybrid Benefit on Business Critical = about 18% off the vCore rate
1-year reserved capacity on the remaining compute = about 11% further
$2,153 + $1,079 = $3,232, rounded down to $3,110 for storage that cannot be reserved
resources.risk: Hybrid Benefit requires the licences to have Software Assurance. Finance has confirmed 24 core licences are held and unused. Changing license_type is a metadata update with no restart.
resources.effort: One Terraform apply and one purchase. No downtime.

resources.finding: Queries are billed per terabyte scanned. Volume has sat between 1,150 and 1,220 TiB for four consecutive months, which is stable enough to commit to slots instead. Two scheduled queries also scan full tables where a partition filter would do.

current_config.label: The pattern driving the scans
current_config.code:
-- Scheduled daily, scans the full events table every run
SELECT user_id, event_type, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM `analytics.events`
WHERE event_type IN ('signup','purchase')
GROUP BY 1, 2;

-- events is 41 TB, partitioned on event_date, but the query
-- has no partition filter, so every run scans all of it.

change.label: Filter the partition, then commit to slots
change.code:
-- 1. Add the partition filter (daily job only needs one day)
SELECT user_id, event_type, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM `analytics.events`
WHERE event_date = CURRENT_DATE() - 1
  AND event_type IN ('signup','purchase')
GROUP BY 1, 2;

-- 2. Enforce it so this cannot regress
ALTER TABLE `analytics.events`
SET OPTIONS (require_partition_filter = TRUE);

-- 3. Then buy a baseline slot commitment for the steady volume:
--    bq mk --capacity_commitment --plan=ANNUAL --slots=500

maths: Two scheduled queries scan 41 TB daily where 0.4 TB would do
Wasted scan: 2 x 40.6 TB x 31 days = 2,517 TB, at $6.25/TiB = $735 (already reflected below)
Remaining steady volume after the fix = about 1,060 TiB
500 annual slots = $5,170/month flat, and covers the measured peak
$735 partition saving + $1,455 slot saving = $2,190
resources.risk: Slot commitments cap concurrency. Peak slot usage measured over 90 days was 430, so 500 leaves headroom. require_partition_filter will break any query that omits the filter, which is the point, but it needs an announcement first.
resources.effort: Two query edits, one table option, one purchase. About two hours plus a notice period.

resources.description: Data Lake Gen2, hot tier, 412 TB
resources.finding: All 412 TB sits in the hot tier. Access logs show 78% of the data has not been read in 90 days, and no lifecycle policy exists to move it down.

current_config.label: Lifecycle management policy (current)

change.label: Tier down on age, delete on retention limit

maths: 412 TB total, 321 TB untouched for 90+ days
Hot tier: $0.0184/GB/month. Cool: $0.0100. Archive: $0.0020
Less rehydration allowance for occasional archive reads: -$1,506
resources.risk: Archive tier reads take hours to rehydrate and cost per GB. Only data past 180 days goes there, and the analytics team has confirmed nothing older than 90 days is read interactively.
resources.effort: One policy document. Tiering happens in the background over about 48 hours.

resources.finding: Embeddings are recomputed on every document ingest, including for documents whose text has not changed. A content hash check would skip most of them. Nothing is batched, so everything pays the real-time rate.

current_config.label: ingest/embed.py (current)
current_config.code:
def ingest(doc):
    # Every ingest embeds, whether or not the text changed
    vector = client.embeddings.create(
        model="text-embedding-3-large",
        input=doc.text,
    ).data[0].embedding
    store.upsert(doc.id, vector)

change.label: Skip unchanged text, batch the rest

maths: 41M tokens billed this month
Ingest logs: 62% of documents re-ingested with byte-identical text
Hash check removes 25.4M tokens, but re-embedding after model upgrades still needed
Conservative estimate: 20% token reduction = $1,302
Batching adds no direct token saving, it reduces per-call overhead only
resources.risk: The digest must be invalidated when the embedding model version changes, or stale vectors persist silently. Store the model name alongside the digest.
resources.effort: A small code change plus a schema column. Half a day, and it needs a backfill decision.

resources.finding: A non-production batch scale set with no start/stop schedule. It bills 168 hours a week to serve a team that works about 45. Nothing depends on it outside working hours - the nightly job it was built for was retired in March.

current_config.label: terraform/batch-nonprod.tf (current)

change.label: Scale to zero outside working hours

maths: Running 168 hours a week, needed for about 60 (7am-7pm weekdays)
Idle share: 108 / 168 = 64%
Applying dev/test subscription rates on top would save a further ~$700, not counted here
resources.risk: If anyone has come to rely on it overnight the job will fail at 7pm. Announce, then watch for a week before removing the manual override.
resources.effort: One Terraform apply. The lowest-risk item on this list.

resources.finding: NAT gateway charges per gigabyte processed. Flow logs show 61% of the traffic is application pods reaching Azure Storage and Key Vault - traffic that never needed to leave the virtual network and is only routed through NAT because no private endpoints exist.

current_config.label: terraform/network.tf (current)

change.label: Keep internal traffic inside the network

maths: 38 TB processed at $0.045/GB = $1,752 of the $4,220 (rest is hourly gateway charge)
61% of flows are storage and vault bound = 23.2 TB
23,756 GB x $0.045 = $1,069 removed from NAT
Private endpoints cost $0.01/hour each: 2 x 730 x $0.01 = $15
Plus reduced egress on the storage side: about $126
resources.risk: Private endpoints change DNS resolution inside the VNet. Needs a private DNS zone and a short maintenance window, or name resolution breaks for those services.
resources.effort: Half a day including DNS. Requires a change window.

resources.finding: Nothing to do here, and that is worth stating. The bucket is already on the archive class, has a lifecycle policy, and retention is set by a compliance requirement rather than by choice. Listing it with a zero keeps the analysis honest.
maths: 780 TB at archive class $0.0012/GB = $3,710
The next class down does not exist
Seven-year retention is a regulatory requirement, not a default
